James Frazer. The Scottish anthropologist and classicist whose monumental The Golden Bough synthesized ethnographic reports, folklore, and classical texts into a universal narrative of human intellectual evolution.

Frazer authored The Golden Bough, first published in 1890 and expanded to twelve volumes by 1915. It is an encyclopedic comparative study of mythology, magic, ritual, and religion across cultures. Though his evolutionary framework has been superseded, his collections of comparative mythology and ritual practices remain influential and readable sources.

He proposed that human intellectual history progresses from magic through religion to science. In this scheme, magic rests on belief in sympathetic causation — the idea that similar or contiguous objects affect each other. Religion represents a later stage, involving propitiation of supernatural beings. Finally, science emerges as empirical understanding. This evolutionary thesis was later critiqued by functionalists and relativists, but it shaped early comparative anthropology.

Frazer analyzed the king-priest figure in Mediterranean religion, linking ritualized regicide, fertility rites, and sacral kingship across cultures. The golden bough itself — an object from classical texts — became his window into these practices and beliefs.

Frazer conducted no fieldwork himself. Instead, he synthesized secondary sources, a method characteristic of early comparative anthropology but later seen as methodologically limited. Anthropology would move toward requiring direct fieldwork as essential to the discipline.

His notion of sympathetic magic influenced later anthropological theories of symbolism and ritual. His work also became influential in early modernist literature and psychology, reaching audiences far beyond anthropology through writers like T.S. Eliot and thinkers like Sigmund Freud.
